segments.text: AARON JACOBSON: All right, so why don't we dive in?
We can't start talking about enterprise AI
unless we really set what the landscape is.
And each of you have a very unique perspective
given the businesses that you're running.
Just to start, I would love to really understand what
is the state of enterprise AI?
If you believe Gartner, Gartner says less than 10% of businesses
have agentic AI deployed today, and by 2030, that
will be over 80%.
Based off of your perch, looking to the enterprise,
do you agree with that, or do you think it's less?
Does it match up with what you're seeing?
And what you're seeing enterprises do with AI.
Let me start with Duncan.
DUNCAN LENNOX: Sure, yeah.
I think it sounds rough and tumble to me.
It feels like in the last year or two,
I think a lot of enterprises have
done a lot of pilots, done a lot of experimentation,
maybe have one or two agents in production,
but have struggled a little bit with how do we scale that
out and up, breadth and depth.
And I think a lot of that speaks to,
you need a lot more than just a really good model to do that.
A lot of the things that the last-- three of us
have all touched on different areas of it.
But I have a lot of optimism that we are really figuring
those things out right now.
And you can feel that acceleration
starting to take off.
So 80% in 2030 doesn't seem unachievable to me.
AARON JACOBSON: How about you?
RAO SURAPANENI: Yeah, mine is probably
a little bit self-selected cohort that I talked to.
So I'm definitely seeing a lot of adoption,
especially when the organizations have figured out
their data governance and security posture,
they're able to move faster.
So I talk to a lot of those customers, learn from them,
and then help the customers who are figuring it out.
They could be figuring it out on how
to train the people to use this or how
to train their internal compliance
teams on where they can accept risk
and where they want to move forward faster.
So from my perspective, I'm seeing a lot of adoption.
Use cases vary.
So depending on the risk acceptance and tolerance level,
so I'm seeing good amount of adoption.
ANAHITA TAFVIZI: Yeah, I'd say we're
seeing a lot of customers at different parts of the adoption
curve.
But broadly speaking, I'd say 2025 maybe
was the year of experimentation, still trying
to figure out whether this thing work, how much is
the hallucination rate?
What is it that you're getting in terms of accuracy?
Can you really trust the outcome?
2026 has been more, they are really
proving ROI and seeing that AI actually
is driving ROI at scale.
And then as we're going towards the rest of the year,
I see more and more really using AI for true business
transformation.
So I'd say broadly, I agree with the direction,
though I would say the exact percentage isn't really,
I think, relevant, whether it's 70% or 90%.
I don't think the number of agents
is really the right metric to look at, but really, like,
what's the true business value that you're ultimately
getting from using these agentic AI solutions.
And more and more, we are seeing customers,
as you mentioned, with the right data foundation,
with the right security and governance in place
to get into that direction.
AARON JACOBSON: Adarsh.
ADARSH HIREMATH: Yeah, I would say
that I think so far enterprise adoption has been underwhelming,
but that trend will change very, very quickly.
And we're already seeing it in 2026.
And there's two reasons for that.
One is largely a willingness thing,
which is that, for the past 10 years,
automation and business transformation has just
been pitched in different forms, everything from BPO,
task mining, process mining.
So there's just a long--
there's a big graveyard of failed pilots and initiatives
there.
So I've noticed that a lot of enterprise executives
are a little bit hesitant about AI transformation
because it's one of those things, at least initially.
And then the second thing is just a capability problem,
where the models just weren't good enough until very recently.
I think the big shift is towards the agentic paradigm, where
it's no longer models for chat use cases.
It's models for essentially being a coworker, which
means managing many different stakeholders, data sources,
and delivering economically valuable work
output versus being a personal assistant.
So I'm optimistic about that 10% number, or whatever number,
going up very quickly.
SUROJIT CHATTERJEE: I think there are two things-- first,
the definition of adoption itself.
I think there's a lot of token maxing, a lot of people
using AI as personal agents as Rao was talking about.
I don't quite think that should be considered an enterprise
adoption because a lot of those projects are failing or low ROI.
But if you look deeply at true workflow end-to-end automation,
I think the 10% number is probably right.
But it's growing fast, much faster
than I would have expected.
In fact, in Fortune 2000, there is a real appetite now
to go and agentically transform their businesses.
So that's the first thing.
I'm actually more optimistic.
I think we may hit that 80% number even earlier than 2030.
The second point is it's not--
where the adoption actually kind of stops,
it's not so much technical anymore.
It used to be-- it was technical.
I think last year or a few years back.
70% reason is organizational.
It's the change management.
It's security, infosec, fear of unknown, and so on.
So I think if we can cross that chasm
of organizational resistance, so to say,
we'll see faster adoption.
AARON JACOBSON: So Surojit, you make an interesting point,
what does adoption mean?
I think the other big question I have in AI
is, what does success look like?
Anahita, you talked about ROI.
When you're out there talking to enterprises,
how are they measuring ROI?
What's interesting to customers?
Are they looking for additional revenue?
Are they looking for cost-savings?
Is this really a question of employee productivity?
Where do you think the most interesting value
that's going to be created for AI is today that's
resonating with enterprises?
ANAHITA TAFVIZI: Ultimately, when we talk about ROI,
we always say there are two ways that you deliver ROI.
Either you help customers make more money or spend less money.
So you want to either increase productivity or help them
deliver additional revenue.
It is extremely difficult to get to that bottom-line measurement.
So companies are using a variety of metrics--
AARON JACOBSON: Let's try it.
We'll try going to a different panelist then,
so we can get Anahita's his mic working again.
So Duncan, maybe you could talk a little bit
about how do you all measure ROI and success within HubSpot.
I know you're bringing-- how are you
sharing that with enterprises that you're bringing AI to?
DUNCAN LENNOX: We try to really stay focused on,
here comes the new boss, same as the old boss, which
is outcomes-- at the end of the day,
really understanding specifically
what are the business outcomes we're trying to drive.
We can look across, say, the go-to market journey
and identify whether it is a new qualified lead
into the top of the funnel.
It is a close one deal.
It is a customer support ticket resolved successfully
for the customer.
And that brings a level of clarity
to how we build, obviously, agents
under that to deliver those.
It also lets you turn it into a metric,
because if you can't measure it, you're
not going to be able to measure success at all.
And we found that to work very well
and basically paint the picture for our customers of what's
the core high-level outcomes are across the journey.
And then you can start filling in the pieces along the way.
AARON JACOBSON: I want to bring you back to Anahita
now that hopefully her mic is working.
ANAHITA TAFVIZI: Yes, I believe this one is working.
We were talking about how do we measure ROI.
And I mentioned that ultimately, you
want to measure the impact on the bottom line.
But it's very difficult because when
you make an improvement in one of your workflows,
measuring what gets you there ultimately to the bottom line
takes time.
So companies are using a variety of leading indicators,
whether it started with adoption,
and token consumption, which was certainly not a good use of ROI,
token maxing as Surojit suggested.
But now it's more and more we are seeing measurements
of the length of workflow.
Has it gotten shorter?
I'll give you an example.
One of the agents that we built, for example,
shortened our quarterly reporting
from two weeks to 48 hours, or our earnings prep from weeks
of work to just a couple of hours of work,
or customer preparations for from weeks to minutes.
So that's how we're starting to measure productivity
at the workflow level.
But I expect as more and more we get
to full automation and full workflow transformation,
we should be able to see full impact on the bottom line.
AARON JACOBSON: Yeah, I think another key part of getting ROI
out of AI is simply actually getting AI into production.
And Adarsh, in your talk, you mentioned
how most enterprises are actually failing and getting
AI off the ground.
Gartner says that 50% of GenAI projects fail.
In your experience, Adarsh, why is that?
Is it a technology challenge, or is it the technology
is not good enough?
Or do you see it as an organizational adoption
where this technology is so new organizations are still
figuring out how to actually deploy this?
ADARSH HIREMATH: Yes, I would say there's a couple of things.
So the first one is just the actual confidence in the fact
that the AI is performing the way you want it to.
And our thesis there is just that most of these enterprises
don't have robust evaluations that are agentic,
meaning they have the task, the trajectory, the context,
the artifact, and the verifier across all of it
to make sure that you actually know
the agent is doing what you want it to before it
hits any production context.
So that's the first thing.
The second thing is, for AI adoption to be successful,
you just can't hurl software over the fence.
It needs to come with change management, cultural changes,
all of these different things.
So it's actually a little bit involved,
which is why you're seeing a lot of the labs
spin up their own deploy codes with these FDEs
and partners with these consultants
and all of this sort of stuff.
Because doing a business transformation
when your whole culture is not AI forward,
not technology forward is really, really hard.
And I anticipate that more of those
involved end-to-end full-stack deployment
efforts will increase the amount of AI adoption
and successful pilots.
AARON JACOBSON: And Surojit, how about you?
What's been your experience when you're talking to enterprises
when it comes to actually helping
them get AI off the ground?
SUROJIT CHATTERJEE: Absolutely.
So giving a real example, one of our customers,
they have around 250,000 employees worldwide across 65
countries.
And they implemented our AI employees
for the entire hire-to-retire cycle process,
like sourcing, recruiting, onboarding, and employee, all
of their IT needs, ITSM-type things, payroll questions,
and also actually managing payrolls and so on.
So AI employee is taking actions,
answering questions across around 70-odd use cases.
And we did this over a course of three or four months for them.
The impact-- and this came from top down.
So the impact is actually real.
So from 1,000 employees-- they had around 1,000 people
in their HR ops team.
They cut it down to almost 500 people,
from five days to resolve an employee question to five
seconds or 10 seconds, average, to resolve an employee question.
So real actual productivity gain,
real employee happiness gain.
So they see a 20% increase in employee satisfaction
for all issues related to employee issues,
employee questions and so forth.
So I think this shows that if there is a will, it can happen.
But it required, as others say, a lot of change management.
The biggest change management was training their employees
to adapt to the new systems, new processes
rather than go back to the old systems.
Very quick, funny anecdote--
30% of the queries the employees would do--
their CHR who told me, and this is company is called Wipro.
They're global professional services company.
30% request, the employees actually ask a human again,
even though AI agents already answered or resolved
the issue, resolved the ticket.
So they were very curious, what was the issue?
So they did some survey and focus groups.
Apparently, employees didn't trust agents can actually do it.
So they wanted a human to confirm, again,
that this was correct.
So over time, there's a lot of education
involved in educating the employees to adopt
an agentic solution.
AARON JACOBSON: Yeah, I love that you brought up
this question of trust.
Do the users trust the AI?
And there's also this question, should enterprises trust AI?
Rao, you talked about this in your talk.
What do you make of the security challenges?
Do you think AI is actually trustworthy today?
Is it trustworthy?
But we're still winning over.
Enterprises are still convincing themselves
that AI should be trusted and figuring out
how to deploy AI securely.
We'd love to hear your thoughts there.
RAO SURAPANENI: I definitely see trustworthy.
At the same time, trust but verify.
Coding became amazing because you're
able to verify, verify programmatically, or maybe even
deploy another agent to verify.
So the solutions where you able to do this, both generate
as well as verify, is where we are seeing accelerated adoption.
I'll use a different example, sales.
One of my customers, his focus is
I want my sales team just selling.
Everything that they do before and everything
that they do after, I want to be able to automate with agents.
He's able to trust the AI to do the right research, to summarize
the meeting prep, and use our notebook LLM to create
a podcast so that they can listen on their drive
to the customer site.
So simplify all of that, and you're just having
the conversation well prepared.
Have that conversation.
And then post that, you're able to update the meeting, CRM,
whatever you need to do.
When there are solutions in place that can help you verify,
we are able to trust much more.
And it is also about the people's own journey
in how they get to that stage of,
this is providing enough value, so I can take some risk here.
And I will trust this content and then go with it.
AARON JACOBSON: Duncan, does that match up
with your experience running security within HubSpot?
the rough edges-- how have you experienced the rough edges
of AI?
And how do you make sure that you're
deploying AI securely for your enterprise customers?
DUNCAN LENNOX: Yeah, I think there's two sides to it.
On the one hand, models, sophisticated as they are,
are just weights in code.
So everything we've done for a long time around trust
and safety and security, those practices all apply,
including things understanding the different outcomes require
different levels of trust and how we watch out for that,
if you will, along the way.
I think it's also interesting, though, that whilst we
can take these frameworks that we've had
and leverage them in the LLM world-- on the other hand,
a bunch of the conversation we've had here
is all roads lead back to high-quality evals.
And I 100% think that is true.
The challenge that I think is underestimated
is unlike a lot of other change management or previous tech
transformations, even like the cloud or mobile,
we were really coming up with a different way
of doing things or accessing things
that was very easy to grok, that you could wrap
your head around what it was.
And I think that's much harder with this transformation.
So if you take evals and that's not just
the new version of QA and test coverage,
there's a skill around being able to write good evals, what
a good, high-quality golden sets look like and, so forth.
Mercor, obviously, does a ton of great work in this space.
But that's a whole skill that people
need to learn in order to be successful.
And figuring out how we get people
through that change, I think, is critical.
AARON JACOBSON: Yeah, I think evals is a great example.
And it actually leads into our next question.
And I can open this up to the panel more broadly.
Besides evals, what are you seeing
working for enterprises who are successfully deploying AI?
Is there a specific use case?
Is there a specific model architecture, one model,
many models?
Would love just to hear from you all experience.
What are you seeing as some of the early signs of success
and what it takes to succeed with AI in enterprise?
SUROJIT CHATTERJEE: I can take it, unless you--
where we see most success today, a couple of areas-- of course,
customer support, employee experience, employee support,
which is two sides of it, kind of support.
We see a lot of examples of finance operations today,
invoice processing, APR, and data extraction, basically
document-heavy use cases, any document-heavy use cases.
I'm expecting the surface area continuously expand over time.
And we are seeing that once we get into a large enterprise,
they will ask for more help in adjacent areas.
In terms of architecture, everyone
is realizing depending on a single model
is not the way to go because the models are
kind of getting better.
There's a war of attrition on models.
And I think the model layer is going to be commoditized.
And open source models are getting better.
So for us, for example, we use ML fusion,
which blends 100-plus models, all frontier models,
many open source models.
And customers can take advantage of that.
But I think that some kind of model fusion
is becoming standard architecture choice.
Of course, I'll let others comment on other pieces.
AARON JACOBSON: Anahita, did you want to speak to that?
ANAHITA TAFVIZI: Maybe I can add to that a little bit.
Yeah, so broadly, we're seeing it
across multiple functions across enterprises.
As Surojit said, customer support
is a very highly well-defined workflow
that we have seen a lot of automation.
And that finance similarly, well-defined workflows,
especially quarter close, month close, all of those
are like well-defined processes that needs to be followed,
highly automatable.
And we have seen a lot in go-to market teams-- sales,
because they are the drivers of revenue.
When you increase efficiency there,
you increase your top-line, marketing,
because there are huge budgets we are talking about,
and then customer support and finance,
as I mentioned, because those are
highly automatable solutions.
But we are seeing it across different industries,
across different verticals, and across different functions.
Maybe one thing I'll also bring back on that trust question
that you said.
When we talk about trust, there are two elements
that we primarily focus on.
One is, can you trust that the data is accurate?
And its accuracy, basically.
So for example, if I ask an agent what was my Q1 revenue,
there's only one correct answer.
And this is not a trivial solution
to a nondeterministic technology by nature.
So putting the right guardrails and the right evals
and the right definitions in place
to ensure that you always get that accurate answer
and that you can trust this is highly important for enterprise
AI adoption.
Because ultimately, if you want every employee
to use these agents, as opposed to humans,
to get basic questions answered, you
need to make sure that there is accuracy there 100% of the time.
The other option is dashboards, which, by default,
have that level of accuracy.
The second one is governance, so how
do you ensure-- especially for data agents,
how do you ensure that the right people can have access
to the right data and not beyond that?
When you're opening up access to your financial data
across the organization, to your employee compensation data,
to your performance data, how do you
make sure that each sales account executive only
gets access to the portion of revenue
that they are supposed to see?
How do you ensure that each manager
sees the data for their own employees, but not their peers.
So those are the two elements that we focus on
that I believe is a non-negotiable for enterprise
AI adoption.
AARON JACOBSON: Rao, you guys are probably
working with some of the largest organizations in the world.
What's the Google perspective?
Where are you seeing some of the early takeoff with the AI,
and any commonalities of success within your enterprise
customers?
RAO SURAPANENI: Yeah, a lot to do with the employee
productivity, really, stemming from finding
the right information at the right time for what
you're trying to do.
Surfacing information is one thing, and then taking
the action.
What's the benefit policy on something to actually completing
that action to enroll for it.
So we are able to automate those extensively with the Gemini
Enterprise product.
And on the other extreme, CIOs are going deep.
I use the sales team example, where
they're able to automate every single task that a specific role
is doing, and they're able to deliver that exceptionally well.
Now, they're actually measuring sales productivity.
Are they able to have more conversations,
and are they able to close more deals faster, aside
from the usual employee delight and those kind
of factors as well?
So we're seeing it across the employee productivity, as well
as actual delivering business ROI.
AARON JACOBSON: So, Anahita, I want to bring it
back to something you said.
Actually, it'll be a question for Adarsh,
given what he was talking about earlier.
But let's talk about data, and let's
particularly talk about sovereign AI.
Should enterprises keep their data?
Should they share their data with Frontier model providers?
Should enterprises run their own models?
The Palantir CEO recently argued that AI model companies,
they pose a threat to most enterprises.
Is that an overplayed geopolitical angle?
Or do you think sovereign AI actually matters to enterprises?
Adarsh, you mentioned earlier how you guys
are going to the enterprises.
You help enterprises unlock using AI with their data.
What do you view of sovereign AI?
When you look across the data layer, the model
layer, confidential compute layer,
what do you think it's OK for enterprises
to share versus what should stay behind their firewall?
ADARSH HIREMATH: Yeah, so I think
there's a couple of moving parts to the question.
But the first thing which is how are enterprises going
to harness their own data to make these model deployments
work, I very much subscribe to the school of thought
that every enterprise is definitionally idiosyncratic.
Even for two companies in the same space, McKinsey and Bain,
each of them have their own processes
that make them special.
And if they're exactly one to one the same,
then neither of them would exist.
There would only be one entity that subsumes both of them.
So I think the implication for a lot of AI adoption
and deployment is that the hardest part is encoding
a lot of that unique secret sauce of the company, which
is the workflows, processes, and organizational context
into the actual model weights or the harness.
And it can be something as sophisticated as a way
that an insurance company does underwriting.
Or we all know that AI agents can review resumes,
but you can't just deploy an agent
to do that unless the agent knows what is the talent
philosophy of that company, how do
hiring managers of that company screen for resumes,
and stuff like that.
So that in general, the challenge
of encoding the company specific context and intelligence
into the model, into the agent, I believe
is very, very challenging to get right
and the most important thing for these deployments to go well.
Now, the second point, which is about the sovereign AI,
what data is OK to share, and so on and so forth--
we work with a bunch of companies
who are sharing what we call commodity workflows with the AI
labs.
So a lot of the AI labs are looking
to just see how well the models can actually
improve model capability in real enterprise contexts.
So for example, an IT function, if you
want to make the agent really good at traversing
all of the different parts of your IT stack,
we can help anonymize the data, do the identity scrubbing,
put it in an RL environment that's
useful to the labs for training.
And that's typically a no-cost option for the average company
because we can generate on the order of magnitude of seven
or eight figures for them by monetizing their data very,
very effectively.
Now, the last thing, which is on the open weights stuff,
I think there are going to be a bunch of use
cases for private models.
I think there's going to be a bunch of use
cases for open-source models because it
hits the price-performance curve a lot better.
And the only way to figure out which one is right is evals.
AARON JACOBSON: So I'd love to get the model provider
view on this.
Rao, you are one of those model providers.
Not to put you on the spot, but do
you think the Palantir CEO is correct?
Should enterprises be sharing their data
with Google and other model providers?
Can they trust you all that you'll
use the data in the right way and won't compete with them?
RAO SURAPANENI: Yeah, you can absolutely
trust Google to do that.
So building on what Adarsh is saying,
so there is enterprise data, but depends
on whether you can give that data to the agent.
It doesn't always need to be in the model.
So you can give it in prompts.
You can give it in context.
I view it as, the best context is the smallest
context that gets the job done.
So you actually can do a lot of things
in a sovereign environment using a frontier model.
You have all of that control.
And obviously, the enterprise agreements that we have,
we don't see the customer's data.
So as an enterprise, that's sacrosanct for us as well.
Frontier models will continue to improve.
And then customers understanding the cost, performance,
and latency, and we always try to be
the best on the Pareto chart.
The customers do and will use a variety of models.
And we try to provide all the flavors for it.
You have the Gemini Pro, Flash, and Flash-Lite
to find the right use case for the right model.
That's on how enterprise can keep their data
and still use frontier models.
Coming back to the open-source models, what that is doing today
is it's eliminating the cost of training for an enterprise.
But the cost of inference is still a cost.
Especially compared to a CPU and the newer workloads,
you still have a much higher marginal cost when you're
actually running the model.
So as an enterprise, you have to ask yourself,
am I willing to invest in that capex?
Am I willing to invest in the people and the capabilities
to grow that over time?
So there are multiple elements here
to deal with when you're thinking open source does not
solve everything.
So you want to also think about the business
aspects and the organizational expertise when you think about,
am I doing it on my own?
AARON JACOBSON: So I love that you brought up
open source again.
And Surojit mentioned it earlier.
So to close the panel out, I'd love to dive
into this question of open versus closed.
If you follow X, it seems like open source
has won the hearts and minds of everybody on X.
Is that what you're seeing within the enterprise?
Do enterprises care about open versus closed?
If you think about five years from now,
who's going to win the model battle within enterprise?
Is it going to be open?
Is it going to be closed?
Is it going to be both?
Maybe Duncan, you can start us off
given you've actually built and deployed AI systems.
What's your view on open versus closed?
What are you using internally, and do you
think enterprise customers care about either?
DUNCAN LENNOX: I think at the end
of the day, what enterprise customers care
about is trust and reliability.
And it's all about how do you solve for trust and reliability.
And that probably means you don't
want to have any single point of failure in the critical path,
if you think of it as an engineering system,
even as a business system.
So I think driving the right outcomes, which
are going to be that balance of cost and performance
and reliability, and so forth-- and there won't
be a single thing that is the right one for any of those.
So I think we'll absolutely continue to see a mix of those.
And we'll get more sophisticated about the tooling
that we use to be able to bring those to bear.
And again, make sure we've got reliability
without any single point of failure anywhere in the chain.
AARON JACOBSON: Anahita, I'd love
to get your view because I know Snowflake works has
their own open models.
You work with frontier model providers.
What do you think the future of AI in the enterprise looks like?
ANAHITA TAFVIZI: Yeah, we work with both.
And I'd say the future is probably a combination of both.
What we are seeing today is frontier models so far has been
the more innovative models.
They're a bit ahead of everybody else.
They're pushing the boundaries of technology and innovation
forward.
Open source models give you better cost,
brings more competition, and increases innovation
as a result of that, and gives you
better auditability and visibility into what's
happening under the hood.
And I think for different workflows you probably need
different one of these models.
If you're just simply summarizing an email,
you probably don't need the most advanced reasoning model,
whereas there may be certain tasks for which you actually
want the most advanced reasoning model.
So I said the future is really providing both of them
to the customers and helping them dynamically route
the queries to the right model.
And that's what we're doing at Snowflake, providing
that flexibility to the customers
to optimize at the query level for the right model
that they want to use for that specific use case.
AARON JACOBSON: And Surojit, I'm going
to let you close it out because you
mentioned open-source models.
You said you think 40%/50% of your internal work is open
source.
What's your view on where open source is
headed versus frontier?
SUROJIT CHATTERJEE: I agree with Anahita.
I think the question is about-- the strategic question is,
can you change your model?
It's not open source versus closed source.
And if you change your model, do you need
to change your entire stack?
Will it break apart, fall apart?
Do need to code everything again?
To build correctly, you should build in a way
that you can change your model, or you
have some kind of a model blender, model selector
underneath your agentic orchestrator
